Goal: safely and efficiently return client to pre-illness baseline strength and work capacity over 3 weeks while respecting persistent fatigue and recent 4 kg weight loss. Emphasize progressive loading, conservative intensity, higher emphasis on recovery, nutrition to regain body weight and support immune recovery. Keep sessions 3–4 per week depending on energy; I'll present a 4-day option with an alternative 3-day reduced volume plan.

Guiding principles
- Conservative intensity start: use ~50–60% of pre-illness 1RM in week 1 for multi-joint lifts, progressing to ~70–80% by week 3 only if client reports improving energy and no unusual soreness.
- Focus on movement quality, mobility, and technique to rebuild confidence.
- Higher relative frequency of key lifts with lower volume per session (e.g., two squat or bench sessions per week but lighter).
- Manage overall training stress: include extra rest between sets, reduce accessory volume if fatigue high, and use autoregulation (RPE/Borg/energy check) each session.
- Nutrition and recovery prioritized: calorie/protein increase, sleep, hydration, light aerobic conditioning.
- Monitor: use daily wellness check (sleep, resting HR, energy, appetite). Stop progression if persistent increased resting HR, worsening fatigue or breathlessness.

Three-week program overview
- Week 1: Reintroduction — low intensity, emphasis on technique, movement prep, metabolic conditioning light. 3–4 sessions (I recommend 4×/week if client tolerates).
- Week 2: Gradual progression — increase intensity and slightly more volume; add heavier single sets but keep overall load conservative.
- Week 3: Return-to-baseline push — reach ~75–80% of pre-illness loads on main lifts if client feels recovered; still avoid 1RM attempts. Aim to recover within-submaximal range so client can resume normal program after block.

Prelim 1RM references (pre-illness)
- Bench 1RM = 100 kg
- Squat 1RM = 140 kg
- Deadlift 1RM = 170 kg

Session structure (approx. 60–75 min)
- Warm-up 10–15 min: general cardio 5–8 min easy (bike/walk), dynamic mobility, specific warm-up sets for main lifts (gradual ramps).
- Main lifts: conservative percentages/sets, rest 2–3 minutes between heavy working sets.
- Secondary compound/assistant lifts: moderate sets, 60–90s rest.
- Accessories: 2–3 exercises, focused on posterior chain, upper back, core; lower volume — 2–3 sets of 8–15.
- Finish: light conditioning 5–10 min (optional) and mobility/cool-down.

Autoregulation rules (simple)
- Rate session RPE (1–10). If energy ≤4/10 or RPE target feels >2 above planned, reduce load by ~10–15% or cut accessory volume in half.
- If resting HR >6–8 bpm above baseline or marked fatigue/new symptoms: skip session or do active recovery (mobility/walk).

4-day per week plan (primary). Alternate 3-day plan shown at end.

Week 1 — Reintroduction (low intensity, low-moderate volume)
- Intensity guidance: main lifts at ~50–60% pre-illness 1RM for working sets. Focus on 2 heavy-but-easy working sets per main lift.

Day A — Upper (Push emphasis)
1. Warm-up + joint mobility, rotator cuff activation.
2. Bench press: 3 warm-up sets, then 2 working sets @55% x 6–8 reps (controlled tempo). Rest 2–3 min.
3. Incline dumbbell press: 3 x 8–10 @ moderate weight (RPE ~6). 90s rest.
4. Seated cable row or chest-supported row: 3 x 8–10. 90s rest.
5. Overhead press (standing or seated): 2 x 6–8 @ light–moderate. 2 min rest.
6. Face pulls: 3 x 12–15. 60s rest.
7. Core: dead bug or pallof press: 3 x 10–12 each side.
8. Optional light conditioning: 8–10 min bike at conversational pace.

Day B — Lower (Squat focus)
1. Warm-up + ankle/hip mobility, bodyweight squats.
2. Back squat: 3 warm-up sets, then 2 working sets @55% x 6–8. Pause reps optional for technique. Rest 2–3 min.
3. Romanian deadlift (RDL) light technique work: 3 x 6–8 (moderate weight) — focus hamstring lengthening. 90–120s rest.
4. Split squat or lunges (dumbbell): 3 x 8 per leg. 60–90s rest.
5. Glute bridge or cable pull-through: 3 x 10–12. 60s rest.
6. Calf raises: 3 x 12–15.
7. Core: plank 3 x 30–45s.

Day C — Upper (Pull emphasis)
1. Warm-up + thoracic mobility.
2. Bent-over row (or Pendlay depending on back): 3 warm-up sets, 2 working sets @55–60% x 6–8. 2–3 min rest.
3. Lat pulldown or pull-ups (assisted if needed): 3 x 6–10.
4. Incline DB press or floor press (light): 3 x 8–10 (a second chest stimulus but lighter).
5. Single-arm dumbbell row: 3 x 8–10 per side.
6. Rear delt fly / band pull-aparts: 3 x 12–15.
7. Core: hanging knee raises or cable crunch 3 x 10–12.
8. Optional 8–10 min walk/row easy.

Day D — Lower (Deadlift/Posterior chain)
1. Warm-up + hip hinge drills.
2. Deadlift (conventional): work up to 2 working sets @55–60% x 4–6 (stop well short of failure). Long rests 2–3 min.
3. Front squat or goblet squat: 3 x 6–8 at light–moderate.
4. Good mornings or back extension (weighted light): 3 x 8–10.
5. Single-leg Romanian deadlift: 2–3 x 8 per leg.
6. Core: farmer carry 3 x 30–60s (light-moderate load).
7. Mobility / foam rolling.

Notes Week 1
- Keep session density moderate. All working sets should feel controlled, RPE 6–7 max.
- Track bodyweight, appetite and resting HR daily.
- Protein target: 1.8–2.2 g/kg bodyweight per day to support regain of lean mass; increase overall calories by ~300–500 kcal/day aiming for gradual regain of lost 4 kg across subsequent weeks (not all within 3 weeks).
- Hydration and vitamin/mineral focus: ensure adequate electrolytes, consider vitamin D and a multivitamin if diet limited. Continue monitoring symptoms from illness.

Week 2 — Progressive reconditioning (moderate intensity, slight volume increase)
- Intensity guidance: aim main lifts at ~60–70% pre-illness 1RM for working sets; increase to 3 working sets where tolerated.
- If persistent fatigue remains, stay at week 1 loads and repeat week 1 with small volume increase for tolerated lifts.

Day A — Upper (Push)
1. Warm-up.
2. Bench press: 3 warm-up sets, then 3 x 5–6 @60% (stop 1–2 reps short of failure). 2–3 min rest.
3. Incline DB press: 3 x 6–8. 90s rest.
4. Seated cable row: 3 x 6–8 heavier than week 1.
5. Overhead press: 3 x 6 @ moderate load.
6. Face pulls: 3 x 15.
7. Core: Pallof press 3 x 10 each side.

Day B — Lower (Squat focus)
1. Warm-up.
2. Back squat: 3 x 5–6 @60% (add a 3rd working set). Rest 2–3 min.
3. RDL: 3 x 6–8 (slightly heavier).
4. Bulgarian split squat: 3 x 6–8 each leg.
5. Hip thrust or glute bridge: 3 x 8–10.
6. Calves, core plank variations.

Day C — Upper (Pull)
1. Warm-up.
2. Barbell row or chest-supported row: 3 x 6 @60–65%.
3. Pull-ups / lat pulldown: 4 x 6–8.
4. Incline DB press light: 2 x 8 (maintain chest volume without overtaxing).
5. Single-arm row: 3 x 8.
6. Rear delt and upper back accessory: 3 x 12–15.
7. Core and 8–10 min low-moderate cardio if energy okay.

Day D — Lower (Deadlift emphasis)
1. Warm-up.
2. Deadlift: 3 working sets @60–65% x 3–5. Focus tempo and set-up. 2–3 min rest.
3. Front squat or goblet: 3 x 6–8.
4. Back extension or glute-ham raise: 3 x 8–10.
5. Single-leg RDL: 2–3 x 8.
6. Farmer carry or loaded carry: 3 x 30–60s.
7. Mobility/cool down.

Notes Week 2
- Aim training RPE ~7 on main lifts; do not push to maximal effort.
- Increase carbs around training (pre/post) to support performance and recovery. Post-workout meal with ~20–40 g protein and 40–60 g carbohydrates soon after sessions.
- Continue protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg and increase total calories if client remains in weight-loss state. If nausea or low appetite persists, consider liquid nutrition (high-protein shakes) to meet needs.
- Ensure sleep hygiene (7–9 hours), reduce late-night stimulants, and manage stress.

Week 3 — Return-to-baseline push (target ~75–80% if recovered)
- Intensity guidance: push to ~70–80% of pre-illness 1RM for primary lifts only if wellness indicators are positive (energy improving, body weight stabilizing/increasing, normal resting HR). Still avoid near-max singles. Keep accessory volume moderate.

Day A — Upper (Push)
1. Warm-up thoroughly.
2. Bench press: 3–4 working sets @70–75% x 3–5 (stop 1 rep short of failure).
3. Incline DB press: 3 x 6.
4. Barbell or chest-supported row: 3 x 6–8.
5. Overhead press: 3 x 5–6.
6. Face pulls and core as before.

Day B — Lower (Squat)
1. Warm-up.
2. Back squat: 3–4 x 4–5 @70–75%.
3. Romanian deadlift or good morning: 3 x 6–8.
4. Bulgarian split squat: 3 x 6 per leg.
5. Glute bridges and calf work.
6. Core.

Day C — Upper (Pull)
1. Warm-up.
2. Barbell row or Pendlay: 3 x 4–6 @65–70%.
3. Pull-ups: 4 x 6–8 (weighted only if energy is good).
4. Incline DB press light: 2 x 8.
5. Lateral raises / rear delt work: 3 x 10–12.
6. Core and light conditioning optional.

Day D — Lower (Deadlift)
1. Warm-up.
2. Deadlift: 3 working sets @70% x 3–4 (conservative; use belt if normally used).
3. Front squat or lighter squat variation: 3 x 5–6.
4. Hamstring focus: back extensions or nordics (assisted) 3 x 6–8.
5. Farmer carry / loaded carries: 3 x 40–60s.
6. Mobility.

Notes Week 3
- If client tolerates and feels recovered, aim to re-test single-rep heavy sets near the end of week 3 only when all wellness markers normal. Even then, consider testing 3–5RM rather than 1RM.
- If fatigue persists, drop week 3 intensities back to week 2 or repeat week 2.
- Encourage progressive bodyweight gain: target ~+0.5–1.0 kg over the week if possible (calorie surplus). Prefer whole-food meals with adequate carbs + protein around sessions.

Short answer: not recommended. Even if he feels fine today, jumping straight to pre-illness 1RMs (or full pre-illness loads and intensities) after 3 weeks off with recent flu, persistent fatigue earlier, and 4 kg weight loss carries measurable risks to recovery, immune function, and injury. A safer approach is a conservative step-up (as in the reconditioning block) but you can accelerate progression within that framework if daily wellness stays good.

Why caution is warranted
- Systemic recovery lag: feeling fine one day doesn’t guarantee full physiological recovery. Immune and metabolic systems, sleep, appetite and neuromuscular readiness often recover more slowly than subjective energy.
- Recent weight loss and reduced glycogen: 4 kg loss likely means some glycogen and fluid loss, and lower body mass may limit ability to produce familiar force at previous loads.
- Detraining effects in 3 weeks: neural drive and work capacity decline modestly — heavier loads feel harder. Jumping to heavy singles risks poor technique or inability to complete expected volume.
- Illness/overreach risk: pushing hard too soon increases chance of relapse, prolonged fatigue, or longer recovery time.
- Injury risk: tissue conditioning (tendons, ligaments, connective tissue) also reduces with layoff; sudden high loads increase injury likelihood.

If he truly insists on moving faster, a reasoned compromise
- Don’t go straight to 1RM attempts. Instead treat the first week as an accelerated re-intro using the pre-illness 1RM as reference but reduce volume and leave reps in reserve:
  - Use 80–85% of pre-illness 1RM for multi-set work rather than 90%+ or 100%.
  - Keep working sets fewer (2–3 sets) and rep ranges slightly lower (e.g., 3–5 reps) with 2–3 reps in reserve (RPE ~7–8).
  - Avoid maximal singles, AMRAPs, heavy triples that push to failure.
  - Increase rest between sets (3–4 min for main lifts) and space heavy sessions so lower-body heavy days have at least 48–72 hours before another taxing session.
- Example conservative “accelerated start” loads (based on his pre-illness 1RMs Bench 100 / Squat 140 / Deadlift 170):
  - Bench: 80% = 80 kg for 3 × 4–5 (stop with 2 RIR)
  - Squat: 80% = 112 kg for 3 × 3–5 (stop with 2 RIR)
  - Deadlift: 80% = 136 kg for 3 × 3–4 (stop with 2 RIR)
  - If those feel easy and wellness markers are excellent, progress to 85% later in week (e.g., 85 kg bench, 119 kg squat, 145 kg deadlift) but still keep RPE ≤8 and no singles to failure.
- Keep accessory volume light–moderate, prioritize technique, and maintain aerobic work at easy intensities.

What to monitor closely if you accelerate
- Resting heart rate: an increase of 6–8+ bpm from his baseline over 2 days = down-regulate.
- Sleep quality, appetite, soreness, mood and training RPE: any deterioration → revert to conservative plan.
- Training performance: if reps drop off or bar speed is slow vs expected, reduce load/volume immediately.
- Any respiratory symptoms, breathlessness on light exertion, or fevers — stop and refer to a physician.

Practical coaching cues and adjustments
- Use a conservative warm-up ramp. Don’t assume previous warm-up loads are sufficient when lifting heavier.
- Auto-regulate via RPE/rep backoffs: plan to leave 2 RIR on main sets. If he hits the target reps with 0–1 RIR, keep weight but reduce sets or reduce next session’s load slightly.
- Space heavy lower-body day away from longer run; keep runs easy and short for first week.
- Keep creatine, adequate protein and carbs, and prioritize sleep/nutrition to support heavier training.

Decision framework (simple)
- If he has truly normal energy for 48–72 hours, normal appetite, normal resting HR and no lingering respiratory symptoms, an accelerated start using ~80% with low volume and RIR is reasonable.
- If any signs of fatigue, poor sleep, elevated resting HR, low appetite, or persistent breathlessness appear — revert to the original conservative reconditioning plan.

Clear, simple criteria help decide when to return to full-intensity work after illness and a layoff. Use a combination of objective measures, subjective reports, and gradual testing rather than a single sign. Below are practical signals to monitor and a recommended decision process you can use with your client.

Primary readiness signals (use collectively)
1. Resting heart rate (RHR)
- Trend: RHR returned to his usual baseline (or within ~+3 bpm) for at least 48–72 hours.
- Concerning: sustained elevation >6–8 bpm above baseline over 48 hours → delay heavier work and reduce load/volume.

2. Sleep quality and quantity
- Readiness: consistently getting his normal sleep duration and quality for 3+ nights (e.g., 7–9 hrs, wakes feeling refreshed).
- Concerning: ongoing poor sleep, frequent awakenings or nonrestorative sleep → hold off on high intensity.

3. Subjective energy and recovery
- Readiness: reports good daily energy, minimal persistent fatigue, normal motivation, and appetite for 3–5 days.
- Concerning: persistent low energy, high perceived exertion for easy tasks, or lack of motivation.

4. Appetite and bodyweight trend
- Readiness: appetite returned to normal and bodyweight trending back toward baseline (e.g., stable or up ~0.25–0.5 kg over several days).
- Concerning: continued significant weight loss or poor appetite (may indicate insufficient energy availability).

5. Training performance and neuromuscular markers
- Readiness: bar speed, technique, and reps at conservative loads are similar to pre-illness norms; can complete planned submaximal working sets with expected reps and RPE (leave 1–2 RIR).
- Concerning: marked drop in bar speed, technique breakdowns, or inability to hit planned reps at conservative loads.

6. Respiratory and systemic symptoms
- Readiness: no ongoing cough, breathlessness on mild exertion, chest pain, fever, or other systemic symptoms for at least 7 symptom-free days (or cleared by physician if needed).
- Concerning: any new or persistent cardio-respiratory symptoms — seek medical review before returning to high intensity.

7. Resting and post-exercise recovery heart rate variability (HRV) and subjective recovery scores (if available)
- Readiness: HRV returned near baseline and subjective recovery/wellness scores stable or improving.
- Concerning: sustained depressed HRV or worsening wellness trend.

8. Mood and cognitive function
- Readiness: normal mood, concentration and no brain fog that impairs technique, focus, or safety.
- Concerning: ongoing brain fog, dizziness, or concentration problems.

How to test readiness practically (stepwise)
1. Daily monitoring for 7–10 days
- Track RHR (same time each morning), sleep, subjective energy (1–10), appetite, and training RPE. If most markers are normal and stable for 3–5 days, proceed to step 2.

2. Performance check at conservative loads (2–3 sessions)
- Use 60–75% of pre-illness 1RM for main lifts across 2–3 sessions spaced 48–72 hours apart.
- Criteria to progress: complete planned sets/reps with bar speed similar to pre-illness perception and RPE ≤8 (ideally 6–7), no unusual soreness, and wellness markers unchanged or improved.

3. Submaximal intensity ramp
- Move to 75–85% of pre-illness 1RM for a short block (1 week) with low volume (e.g., 2–3 sets of 3–5) while maintaining 2+ days of recovery between heavy sessions for the same muscle groups.
- Criteria to progress: maintain performance, no RHR elevation, good sleep and appetite.

4. Return to full intensity
- Once he has completed the stepwise ramp (several sessions at 75–85% with stable markers), and feels subjectively strong and recovered, you can reintroduce full-intensity elements (heavy triples, doubles, or 1–3RM testing) — but still prioritize safety: start with 85–90% rather than an immediate 1RM attempt.
- Consider scheduling maximal attempts only after 1–2 weeks of well-tolerated heavy-ish training.

Simple decision rules to use with the client
- If 4 or more readiness signals are positive (RHR near baseline, good sleep, good appetite, normal energy, clean conservative-lift performance), consider moving up intensity cautiously.
- If any “concerning” signals appear (especially sustained RHR elevation, respiratory symptoms, or marked performance decline), pause progression and step back 1–2 weeks to lower intensity/volume and prioritize recovery.

Red flags (stop and refer)
- New or worsening chest pain, breathlessness at rest or with minimal exertion, syncope, or unexplained palpitations — cease high-intensity training and seek medical evaluation.
- Persistent, severe fatigue that does not improve with 7–10 days of reduced training and optimized nutrition/sleep — refer to physician for further assessment.

Practical monitoring tools and cadence
- Daily: morning RHR, sleep hours/quality, 1–10 energy score, and bodyweight (optional).
- Every session: training RPE, bar speed/technical notes, post-session RHR if possible.
- Weekly: trend review — if everything trending positive, move to next intensity step.

Coaching cues when ramping back
- Auto-regulate: insist on leaving 1–2 reps in reserve on heavier sets until multiple indicators are consistently positive.
- Keep accessory volume lower initially and restore over 2–4 weeks.
- Space heavy lower-body sessions to allow 48–72 hours for recovery; avoid piling heavy strength and high-volume runs in the same 48–72 hour window.

Example timeline (typical)
- Week 0–1 post-illness: conservative submaximal loads (50–60%) — monitor markers.
- Week 2: moderate loads (60–75%) if markers good.
- Week 3–4: heavier work (75–85%) with low volume, then test heavy singles after 1–2 weeks of tolerated heavier loading.

When to schedule
- Place the 1RM testing session in the latter half of Week 3 — ideally 48–72 hours after the last heavy lower-body session and after a light day or rest day.

Pre-test day(s)
- 48 hours before: light training or rest, easy short run only if used, good nutrition (slightly higher carbs), hydrate well, sleep priority.
- Test-day morning: normal breakfast with carbs + protein, no heavy cardio, avoid stimulants > usual. Take creatine as usual.
- Brief wellness check 1–2 hours pre-lift: RHR, sleep, energy (1–10). If energy ≤6/10 or RHR elevated >+5 bpm on the morning of test, postpone.

Testing session structure and safety
- Coach present and attentive for spotting and cueing. Use safety equipment: collars, rack safety pins, belt if he normally uses one, and appropriate spotters for bench and squat heavy attempts.
- Warm-up: active 10–15 min general warm-up (bike/walk), dynamic mobility and specific movement prep.
- Follow structured ramping warm-up for each lift; never jump large percentages between attempts. Rest 3–5 minutes between heavy ramp sets and 4–6 minutes between maximal attempts if needed.

Bench press 1RM protocol (example ramp)
- Warm-up sets (strict):
  - Empty bar x 8
  - 40% 1RM (40 kg) x 5
  - 55% (55 kg) x 3
  - 70% (70 kg) x 2
  - 80% (80 kg) x 1–2
  - 90% (90 kg) x 1 (only if bar speed good and technique perfect)
- Attempts:
  - Attempt #1: 95% (95 kg) — if moved with good mechanics and 2–3 RIR then you might skip to #2; otherwise take next attempt.
  - Attempt #2: 100% (100 kg) — if this feels solid; otherwise adjust down/up 2.5–5 kg depending on how attempt #1 felt.
  - Attempt #3: +2.5–5 kg over previous if attempt #2 was confident and RPE ≤9 (only if all readiness metrics remain good).
- Auto-regulation rules:
  - If speed is slow and technique breaks on any attempt, stop further increases and accept the previous successful max.
  - If he misses a lift, reduce next attempt by 2.5–5 kg (don’t chase with big jumps).
  - Keep total number of maximal attempts per lift to ≤3 to limit systemic stress.

  - Empty bar x 8
  - 40% (56 kg) x 5
  - 55% (77.5 kg) x 3
  - 70% (98 kg) x 2
  - 80% (112 kg) x 1–2
  - 90% (126 kg) x 1 (if good)
- Attempts:
  - Attempt #1: 95% (133 kg)
  - Attempt #2: 100% (140 kg)
  - Attempt #3: +2.5–5 kg if previous felt strong (RPE ≤9)
- Safety:
  - Use pins or spotters and ensure depth standardization. If depth or technique fails, stop.

  - 40% (68 kg) x 3

Summary: 3-week reconditioning plan to return client (41M, intermediate) from 3 weeks off with mild flu and 4 kg weight loss back to baseline. Includes week-by-week working loads for main lifts (bench/squat/deadlift), rest/recovery guidance, and progressive return-to-running to 10 km. Use autoregulation — if any wellness marker (resting HR elevated >+5–8 bpm vs baseline, poor sleep, low appetite, breathlessness, unusual soreness) appears, reduce loads/volume or pause testing.

Pre-illness 1RM reference
- Bench = 100 kg
- Squat = 140 kg
- Deadlift = 170 kg

General session structure and rules
- Warm-up: 10–15 min general + specific ramp sets.
- Rest between heavy sets: 2–3 min (3–4 min for heavier ramps).
- RPE target: keep working sets around RPE 6–8 (leave ~2 RIR early weeks).
- If energy/markers poor: reduce working load by 10–15% or skip heavy work; prefer underload vs overshoot.
- Nutrition: ~maintenance +300–500 kcal/day; protein 1.8–2.2 g/kg; carbs sufficient to fuel sessions; creatine recommended.
- Cardio: easy, zone 1–2 runs; progress to ~10 km/week by end of Week 3.

Week 1 — Reintroduction (conservative)
Main lift working loads (2 working sets each):
- Bench: 55 kg × 2 sets × 6–8 reps (≈55% 1RM)
- Squat: 77.5 kg × 2 sets × 6–8 reps (≈55% 1RM)
- Deadlift: 92.5–95 kg × 2 sets × 4–6 reps (≈55% 1RM)
Volume: keep accessory volume low–moderate; session count 3–4/week (4 recommended if energy ok).
Rest days: 1–2 full rest days, active recovery (walk/mobility) on off days.
Running (return-to-cardio):
- Goal week total: 6–11 km depending on energy (conservative 6–8 km).
- Structure: 2–3 easy runs (e.g., Mon 3 km, Thu 3 km, Sun 2 km). Keep pace conversational, no intervals.

Week 2 — Gradual progression (moderate)
Main lift working loads (3 working sets where tolerated):
- Bench: 60% 1RM → 60 kg × 3 × 5–6 reps
- Squat: 60% 1RM → 84 kg (rounded from 84) × 3 × 5–6 reps
- Deadlift: 60–65% 1RM → 102–110 kg × 3 × 3–5 reps (choose lower if doubtful; 102.5–105 conservative)
Volume: slightly increased accessory work but still conservative; keep overall weekly training load moderate.
Rest days: prioritize at least 48 hours between heavy lower sessions; 1–2 full rest days.
Running:
- Goal week total: ~8–12 km.
- Structure: increase to 3 easy runs (e.g., Mon 3–4 km, Tue 3–4 km, Thu 3 km). Keep runs zone 1–2, longest single run ≤4 km.

Week 3 — Return-to-baseline push (conditional)
Main lift working loads (3–4 working sets; progress only if wellness good):
- Bench: 70–75% 1RM → target 70–75 kg × 3–4 × 3–5 reps (start 70 kg, progress to 75 kg if feeling strong)
- Squat: 70–75% 1RM → target 98–105 kg × 3–4 × 4–5 reps (start ~98 kg, step toward 105 kg if good)
- Deadlift: 70% 1RM → target 119 kg × 3 × 3–4 reps; can move to 120–130 kg (≈75%) only if recovered
Notes: aim for RPE ≤8 and stop increasing if any negative signals. Maintain controlled accessory volume.
Rest days: 48–72 hours between heavy lower sessions; plan rest/light days around running and testing.
Running:
- Goal week total: reach ~10 km for the week.
- Structure: progress to 2–3 runs totaling ~10 km (e.g., Tue 5 km easy + Mon 3 km + Thu 2 km), or single easy 10 km only if all wellness metrics excellent.

Back-half Week 3 — 1RM testing (conditional)
- Preconditions before testing: at least several days of good wellness markers (RHR near baseline for 48–72 hrs, good sleep/appetite, no respiratory symptoms), and successful recent sessions at 75–85% with normal bar speed.
- Recommended schedule: split tests if possible (Day 1: Bench + Squat; Day 2 — 48–72 hrs later: Deadlift). If testing all in one day, order Bench → Squat → Deadlift and keep warm-up ramps conservative.
- Warm-up/attempt progression: incremental warm-up sets; attempts at 95% → 100% → small + increments (2.5–5 kg). Limit to ≤3 maximal attempts per lift. Auto-regulate: stop increases if technique slows, RPE too high, or RHR/symptoms worsen.
- Post-test recovery: 48–72 hours of light activity; reassess RHR/sleep/energy. Use tested 1RMs to reset training loads (or round conservatively down if testing conditions suboptimal).

Quick load chart (week-by-week working numbers based on pre-illness 1RMs)
- Bench: Wk1 = 55 kg (2×6–8). Wk2 = 60 kg (3×5–6). Wk3 = 70 → 75 kg (3–4×3–5; test 1RM in back half if cleared).
- Squat: Wk1 = 77.5 kg (2×6–8). Wk2 = 84 kg (3×5–6). Wk3 = 98 → 105 kg (3–4×4–5; test 1RM in back half if cleared).
- Deadlift: Wk1 = 92.5–95 kg (2×4–6). Wk2 = ~102–110 kg (3×3–5). Wk3 = ~119–130 kg (3×3–4; test 1RM in back half if cleared).

Monitoring & go/no-go rules
- If resting HR elevated >+6–8 bpm for 48+ hours, drop intensity/volume or pause testing.
- If sleep/appetite/energy remain poor, stay conservative.
- If any chest pain, dizziness, or breathlessness occurs, stop heavy training and seek medical review.

If you want, I can:
- Produce a day-by-day calendar showing which days are lifts, runs and rest for each week,
- Convert all working numbers to exact plate combinations for your gym’s plate increments,
- Or create the follow-up 4-week program using tested 1RM values once you run the test.
